body:
On 1998-02-10 scrapie@rigel.cyberpass.net(scrapie) said:
 sc>Para 84:  "a surrogate activity that is directed toward an
 sc>artificial goal that the individual pursues for the sake of the
 sc>"fulfillment" that he gets from pursuing the goal, not because he
 sc>needs to attain the goal itself."
 sc>This is another great instance of projection, and it requires that
 sc>we accept his earlier assertions about the artificiality of goals
 sc>he doesn't himself approve of.
 sc>It's also interesting, to me at least, to contrast this with the
 sc>considerable body of thought, most clearly defined for me in
 sc>Buddhist teachings but present also in some Jewish and Christian
 sc>teachings, about the utility of recognizing that attaining goals,
 sc>ultimately, is never necessary - it's the act of pursuing them, and
 sc>the state of mind you're in while pursuing them, which
 sc>distinguishes you.
 sc>TK rejects that line of reasoning - and is in fact making a false
 sc>consciousness argument about it.  (To be fair, he's actually not
 sc>saying anything about state of mind when pursuing what he sees as
 sc>legitimate "power process" goals.)

 sc>Para 92:  This is interesting;  he essentially denies moral agency
 sc>to scientists.  A letter published this week in Nature from a group
 sc>of people working on the Convention on Biological Diversity points
 sc>out "Whether or not this protocol will provide for the
 sc>consideration of social and economic issues is as yet undecided."
 sc>This point is made critically - the authors of the letter are
 sc>imploring the larger community of scientists to make that
 sc>consideration an *explicit* goal because they recognize that as it
 sc>now stands, it is an *implicit* goal and they are required to
 sc>consider it but not voice their considerations.
 sc>They are asking to be able to voice these "broader social
 sc>implications" explicitly.  They recognize that they are now being
 sc>given an ethical agency, and that they need to be able to act on it
 sc>in the open.
 sc>In talking with people who I think have worked in what are to me
 sc>genuinely negative fields of research - weapons design at Lawrence
 sc>Livermore, for instance - I find that those who are directing and
 sc>actively engaged in the work are there because they think they are
 sc>doing the right thing for the country, even with all the risks
 sc>their work entails, and that by doing the right thing for the
 sc>country, they do the right thing for the world.  These people are
 sc>actively aware of and engaging their moral agency - in a direction
 sc>which I choose not to.
 sc>The people who seem unwilling to do so are bright people who act
 sc>more in support than in directing the work.  They see employment in
 sc>the field as ethically neutral, as just a legal job, and don't like
 sc>thinking about the costs and benefits of the work.

 sc>Para 96:  Concludes with:  "In order to get our message before the
 sc>public with some chance of making a lasting impression, we've had to
 sc>kill people."  I wonder if TK realizes the extent to which he's not
 sc>made a lasting impression, but has simply become another media
 sc>commodity - even in the hands of some of his supporters.  Unapack
 sc>sends a copy of the Manifesto out with every order of Unabomber
 sc>goods they sell through their site - but I wonder how many of the
 sc>buyers are pitching it and using the stickers merely for their
 sc>admittedly quite good Situationist humor value?
 sc>-Peter
 sc>scrapie@cyberpass.net
Peter has said some interesting things about his motives, above.

His habit from young was to be interlectualy arragant.
Eventually he wraped nature around himself and his values that he had
tested for soundness himself.
Tested with the throughness of a mathmatician and someone who could
handle the discomforts of his cabin life without sneaking back
to the comforts of modern life.

The belief in his views value was and may still be a sort of pride
in a world meant for him, his own world, his own terretary.
Anyone who invaded that terretary with some sign of differant rules/laws
from his own world was condemed, automaticaly.
This condeming helped justify to himself why he could not be a normal person
participating in the normal world.
When really he may have a real mental handicap such as autism that makes
him good at some stuff and bad at sutle socialising skills.

His condeming was what made him king of his world, that he had the power to
condem them and the justification by the powers of reasen.
It was only later as the outside world became needed as he got old and
tired, did he appeal to the worlds powers of reasen to support
him as he had supported his own judgeings of his victems injurys.

At the begining he possibly wanted companionship in his views, but
mostly he didn't seem to want people to understand his views until
the end.
Unless his earliar bombings had some sorts of note indicating them,
but we never saw them due to the FBI useing the notes for toilet paper.

I believe that the writings of priseners are not the only unusual source
of interesting views but also the views of those in the asylms.
